analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent Data Protection Agency to regulate how companies collect and use personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on June 17, 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new independent federal agency, the Data Protection Agency, and give it power over how companies collect, process, and share personal data. It would oversee 'high-risk' practices like automated decision systems, large-scale profiling, biometric and genetic data processing, and targeted advertising based on sensitive characteristics. Companies above modest size thresholds would face fees, periodic examinations, risk assessments, and the possibility of fines, with penalties paid to victims. The agency would also take over the privacy-enforcement duties the Federal Trade Commission currently holds under a long list of existing laws, including the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose personal information is harvested by data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large platforms. The bill would give individuals enforceable rights to access, correct, limit, and delete their data, and would scrutinize automated decisions that affect hiring, credit, insurance, housing, and health care. It would also mandate a public complaint database with multilingual access and a civil-rights office to address discriminatory data practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose data is harvested online

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals rights to access, correct, limit the processing of, and request deletion of their personal data, with the agency empowered to write rules enforcing those rights.

Requires companies to conduct and submit risk assessments and post-deployment impact evaluations for high-risk practices like automated decision systems and large-scale profiling, with oversight of disparate impacts on protected classes.
Establishes a toll-free number, website, and public complaint database in plain language and five languages, and prohibits re-identifying people from anonymized data.
Transfers enforcement of existing federal privacy laws, including the Fair Credit Reporting Act, Gramm-Leach-Bliley, and the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, from the FTC to the new agency.

analysis.who_pays: Large data collectors — data brokers, ad-tech firms, social media platforms, and any commercial entity with over $25 million in revenue or data on 50,000 or more individuals. They would pay assessments to fund the agency, undergo periodic examinations, file reports, and face civil penalties and cease-and-desist orders for violations. Compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers through higher prices or degraded free services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech, and big platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly exempts the agency's rules from cost-benefit analysis and White House review, and gives courts deference to the agency's own interpretations, so the new regulator could issue very broad rules with limited outside check.

The funding and examination thresholds are low — $25 million in revenue or data on 50,000 people — which sweeps in many mid-sized businesses beyond the big tech firms the bill seems aimed at, and fees could raise consumer prices.
The agency would overlap with the FTC, CFPB, FCC, and other regulators that already enforce some of these laws, creating coordination and duplication risks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give Americans real, enforceable control over data that companies currently collect largely without constraint, and would specifically target automated decision-making and biometric profiling where errors can cost someone a job, loan, or apartment. The main costs are compliance burdens on a broad range of businesses and the creation of a powerful new regulator with unusually little external check on its rules. Those are legitimate concerns, but the underlying problem — widespread commercial surveillance of ordinary people — is real and currently almost entirely unpoliced at the federal level.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in June 2021, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended in January 2023, so no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Gillibrand introduced the bill on June 17, 2021, joined by Sen. Brown, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That referral was the last action in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action followed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting, profiling, and selling personal data — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large platforms — are better off, since no new regulator, fees, or examinations were ever imposed. Americans remain with the status quo: privacy enforcement scattered across agencies and little protection against automated decision systems.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Data Protection Act of 2021 and became its only sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in June 2021 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split is recorded; the bill's only two known supporters were Democrats, and the Democratic-led Senate Commerce Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: These companies' business model is collecting, combining, and selling personal data. The bill would subject them to fees, periodic examinations, risk assessments, public complaint lists, and civil penalties for privacy harms — directly constraining that model.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and social media companies
industries.note: Platforms rely on large-scale profiling, automated decision systems, and biometric or behavioral data for advertising revenue. All of these are designated high-risk data practices the new agency could restrict or require auditing of.

The bill would transfer the FTC's authority over major federal privacy laws to the new agency, consolidating enforcement power away from existing regulators while directing the new agency to coordinate with the FTC, CFPB, FCC, and others.
